t: Swap Adjacent in LR String — Two Pointers on the L/R Skeleton
o: The moves 'XL' -> 'LX' and 'RX' -> 'XR' mean an 'L' can slide left past any number of X's, and an 'R' can slide right past any number of X's. Crucially, L's and R's can never cross each other, and neither character is ever created or destroyed. So both strings must have exactly the same subsequence of non-X characters, and each L/R must be able to reach its target position: an L in start may only move left (its index in start must be >= its index in result), and an R may only move right (index in start <= index in result). In Example 1, stripping X's gives "RLRR" for both strings, and pairing positions confirms every L moves only left and every R only right, so the answer is true. In Example 2 the skeletons differ ("X" vs "L"), so it is immediately false. With lengths up to 10^4 we need at least a linear-time check; simulating individual swaps would be far too slow.
k: Removing all X's from both strings must yield identical sequences — L's and R's never cross or vanish.
An 'L' can only move to smaller indices and an 'R' only to larger indices, so when matching the i-th non-X characters, start's index must be >= result's index for L and <= for R.
This reduces the problem to a single linear two-pointer scan with no simulation needed.

a.n: Approach 1: Two Pointers over Non-X Characters
a.i: Walk through both strings simultaneously, skipping X's. Whenever both pointers land on non-X characters, those characters must match. If they are both 'L', the pointer in start cannot be to the left of the pointer in result (an L can't move right); if both are 'R', the start pointer cannot be to the right of the result pointer (an R can't move left). If one string runs out of non-X characters before the other, the skeletons differ and the answer is false.
s: Skip X's in start (advance i) and in result (advance j).
If both pointers are out of bounds, return true; if exactly one is out of bounds, return false.
Check start[i] == result[j]; then if the char is 'L' require i >= j, if 'R' require i <= j; otherwise return false.
a.t: O(n) — each pointer advances at most n times total across the whole scan.
a.sp: O(1) — only two index variables are used.

a.n: Approach 2: Compare Filtered Strings with Index Lists
a.i: A more declarative variant: build the skeleton (string with X's removed) plus the list of indices where each non-X character occurs, for both strings. The answer is true iff the skeletons are equal and for every position k, the direction constraint holds (start index >= result index for 'L', <= for 'R'). This is easier to reason about but uses extra memory.
s: Build filtered strings s and r by dropping X's from start and result.
For each k, record indices of s[k] in start and r[k] in result during filtering.
Verify startIndex >= resultIndex for 'L' and startIndex <= resultIndex for 'R'.
Return true if all checks pass.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to filter and one pass to verify.
a.sp: O(n) — for the filtered strings and index lists.

w: In an interview, lead with the key observation that L's and R's form an invariant skeleton that can never change order, then present the O(1)-space two-pointer solution as the optimal answer; the filtered-strings version is a good stepping stone if you discover the invariant incrementally. Common pitfalls: forgetting to check that both strings end with no leftover non-X characters (e.g., start="RX", result="X"), mixing up the inequality directions (L needs i >= j, R needs i <= j), and assuming equal length alone suffices. Edge cases include strings of all X's (always true), identical strings (true), and a single character mismatch. Likely follow-ups: prove why the conditions are sufficient (any valid relative displacement of L's and R's can be realized by repeated adjacent swaps since they never block each other), or count the minimum number of moves to transform start into result.
